meta: A round tower, moored boats and a hilltop castle on the Rhine at Oberwesel: David Roberts's 1831 watercolor at the National Gallery of Art.
about: A tall round tower with a crenellated top stands on the bank of the Rhine at Oberwesel. Masted boats are moored beside it, and a castle sits on the hill to the left. David Roberts painted this watercolor in 1831 and it was shown that year at the Society of British Artists in London. It later passed through dealers and private owners in London and New York. Mimi and Sanford Feld were the last collectors to own it, and they gave it to the National Gallery of Art in 2020.

meta: Hieronymus Bosch's Haywain Triptych in the Prado, dated by tree-ring research to about 1516, with a traveller painted on the closed shutters.
about: The Haywain Triptych is a big Bosch panel painting, and its central panel is about two metres wide. Bosch signed that panel Jheronimus Bosch. The catalog gives 1512 as the date, but tree-ring research on the wood points to about 1516. Look at the outside of the wings too. When the shutters are closed they show Bosch's Wayfarer in full color. The triptych is now in the Prado in Madrid.

meta: Two old figures lean out of a black background in Goya's Two Old Men Eating Soup, one of his Black Paintings, now in the Prado.
about: Two old figures lean out of a black background. One has a grimacing mouth, and the other has eyes like dark hollows. Goya painted this directly on a wall of his house, the Quinta del Sordo, as one of fourteen Black Paintings. He never meant them for public view. In the 1870s the paint was moved onto canvas under the Prado curator Salvador Martínez Cubells, and Baron Émile d'Erlanger gave the canvases to the Spanish state in 1881.

meta: A fort at a river mouth with a winged banner and an ostrich coat of arms: Jan van Brosterhuyzen's view of Fort Ceulen in the Rijksmuseum.
about: A fort stands at the mouth of a river, and a few Dutchmen and local people gather by a small boat in the foreground. In the sky a winged banner carries the title, with a coat of arms showing an ostrich. The museum dates this view of Fort Ceulen to between 1636 and 1644. Jan van Brosterhuyzen made it as an etching and engraving, and this impression was touched up with brown pen. The print was later used, with a few changes, in Caspar Barlaeus's history of Count Maurits's years in Brazil, published by Joannes Blaeu in 1647.

meta: A woman stands almost full length holding gloves in Hendrik Gerritsz Pot's 1638 portrait, with part of her age lost from the inscription.
about: A woman stands nearly full length and turns slightly to the left, while her face looks straight out at us. She holds a pair of gloves in her left hand and rests her right hand against her stomach. Hendrik Gerritsz Pot painted her in 1638. An inscription in the upper right corner gives that year and her age, but the second digit of the age can't be read. The Rijksmuseum received the painting as a gift from Mr and Mrs Kessler-Hülsmann.

meta: The knight Huon finds Almansaris lying on a couch, a scene from Wieland's Oberon, in Willem Steelink II's 1889 print.
about: The knight Huon comes upon Almansaris lying on a couch. The scene is taken from Oberon by Christoph Martin Wieland. Willem Steelink II made the print in 1889. In the lower left corner of the margin he added a small sprig of thistle. The print is in the Rijksmuseum.

meta: A commemorative sheet for 200 years of the Haarlemmermeer, with a steam engine, model farms and a portrait of Leeghwater, by Edouard Taurel, 1867.
about: This sheet marks 200 years of the Haarlemmermeer. At the bottom the lake is rough and wild, as it was in 1667. A steam engine sits on the right, and above it is a portrait of Leeghwater set between views of two villages. Higher up are a model farm among three other farm types and a school. At the very top stands the town hall of Hoofddorp, built in 1867, between a pumping station at Lijnden and Fort Schiphol. Edouard Taurel made the print.

meta: Two riders on one sheet, prints 46 and 47 of a series of 77 by Abraham de Bruyn, from a stash left on Novaya Zemlya in the 1590s.
about: Two riders share this sheet, each on a walking horse. The one on the left wears royal dress in Russian fashion and carries a sceptre. The one on the right is dressed as a Russian too and holds a morning star and a drum. They are prints 46 and 47 from a series of 77 by Abraham de Bruyn. The Rijksmuseum puts this later edition in its Nova Zembla collection. Willem Barentsz's expedition had brought such prints from Amsterdam as trade goods. They stayed behind in the winter camp. In 1871 the Norwegian Elling Carlsen found the camp's remains.

meta: Vasily Polenov's Moscow Courtyard, painted in 1878 and bought straight from the exhibition by Pavel Tretyakov, now in the Tretyakov Gallery.
about: Polenov painted the courtyard of the house where he rented an apartment, at the corner of Durnovsky and Trubnikovsky Streets in Moscow. The Church of the Transfiguration on the Sand rises behind the buildings, and the outline of another church shows on the right. He sent it to the Peredvizhniki exhibition in May 1878. It was his first work shown there. Pavel Tretyakov bought it right off the wall.

meta: Arnold Böcklin's In springtime, sold in 1976 under the name Summer and bought by the National Gallery of Victoria the next year.
about: Arnold Böcklin's In springtime passed through several German and British collections before it reached Australia. Frau Senator Berg of Freiburg owned it first. Later it was in Frankfurt, Munich and London. In 1976 it came up at Sotheby's in London as Summer, and the dealer Fischer Fine Arts bought it that year. The National Gallery of Victoria purchased it in 1977 for the Felton Bequest, on the advice of Dr Ursula Hoff.

meta: Caravaggio's Christ on the Mount of Olives was destroyed in Berlin in 1945. It once belonged to the Giustiniani brothers.
about: Christ points toward the approaching soldiers while Peter lies asleep and Saint John and Saint James look on. The scene comes from the Gospel of Matthew, on the night Jesus was arrested. The painting hung in Berlin until it was destroyed in 1945. Some have doubted it was by Caravaggio. Wikipedia answers that it is well documented in the collection of the Marchese Vincenzo Giustiniani and his brother Cardinal Benedetto.

meta: Tintoretto's Saint George on a white horse spears a dragon while a woman kneels nearby. William Holwell Carr left it to the National Gallery.
about: Saint George rides a white horse and thrusts a lance at a winged dragon. A woman in a blue gown kneels close by, and a nude figure lies on the grass in the foreground. Behind them a fortified castle rises beside the sea. Tintoretto painted it in 1555 or 1558. Nobody seems sure which. The collector William Holwell Carr owned it and left it to the National Gallery when he died.

meta: Rembrandt drew Kostverloren Castle after a fire, around 1652, with a felled tree across the foreground. It now belongs to the Art Institute of Chicago.
about: The Kostverloren estate had a name that means lost expenses, or more loosely, money pit. Its owners seemed to suffer one misfortune after another. Rembrandt and his contemporaries were fascinated by that. After a fire destroyed much of the castle, Rembrandt walked onto the grounds and drew what was left. The Art Institute of Chicago says the felled tree in the foreground stresses the decay, and its hard horizontal line sets off the castle's once grand buildings.

meta: Kandinsky's Improvisation No. 30, also called Cannons, painted in 1913 and given to the Art Institute of Chicago in 1931 by the Eddy family.
about: Kandinsky described his improvisations as unconscious, spontaneous expressions, and he made them between 1910 and 1914. This one carries the name Cannons. In a letter to his Chicago friend and collector Arthur Jerome Eddy, Kandinsky said the cannons could be explained by the constant war talk of the year. But he added that the true content is what viewers feel under the effect of the forms and colors. Eddy's family gave the painting to the Art Institute of Chicago in 1931.

meta: Several young boys on a sandy riverbank, some undressed and some still in overalls: Alexander Grinager's Boys Bathing, painted in 1894.
about: Several young boys gather on a sandy riverbank. Some are undressed and some still wear overalls and white shirts, and their clothes lie scattered on the sand in the foreground. Sunlit water and a wooded far shore stretch out behind them. Alexander Grinager painted the scene in 1894 with loose brushwork. He and his wife kept it in New York until they gave it to the Minneapolis Institute of Art in 1947.

meta: A woman in a patterned kimono sits on a bench with a striped fan in Kitao Shigemasa's woodblock print Clearing Breeze from a Fan, about 1772.
about: A woman in a patterned kimono sits on a yellow wooden bench and looks down at a red-striped fan in her hand. Behind her are a blind, a shoji window and a potted flower arrangement, and a poem is written in the upper right. Kitao Shigemasa made the color woodblock print around 1772. The American collector Ernest Fenollosa once owned it. His widow sold it in 1909 to Clarence Buckingham of Chicago, and Buckingham's sisters gave it to the Art Institute in 1925.

meta: Mary Magdalene reaches toward the risen Christ among ruins in Alessandro Magnasco's Noli Me Tangere, about 1705 to 1710, at the Getty.
about: Mary Magdalene kneels before the risen Christ, the first person to see him after the Resurrection. He tells her not to touch him, which is the Latin of the title, and sends her to tell his disciples. Alessandro Magnasco filled this tall canvas, and its pendant Christ and the Samaritan Woman, with classical ruins whose shapes echo the curves of the figures' poses. The Getty describes his brushwork as nervous and sketchy.

meta: Lucas Cranach the Elder's Judgment of Solomon, 1517, a crowned king with two lions beside him and an executioner raising a sword over an infant.
about: A crowned king sits on a throne with a lion on each side. In front of him a red-clad executioner raises a sword over an infant. A kneeling woman in red clasps her hands and pleads. Lucas Cranach the Elder painted the scene of Solomon's judgment in 1517. Berlin acquired the painting in 1821. From 1884 to 1936 it was on loan to the art academy in Düsseldorf.

meta: A woman in a white gown stands by an open piano forte holding printed music in Adèle Romany's portrait, painted in 1808.
about: A woman in a white empire-waist gown and a red coral necklace stands beside an open piano forte. One hand rests on its keys. In the other she holds a rolled collection of printed music, and an open score sits on the music stand. Adèle Romany painted her in 1808. In the 1950s it was sold by the Maison Jansen in Paris to a Brazilian family, the Scarpas. They put it up at Christie's in New York, and the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston bought it in 2014.

meta: Three peasants gather around a table at an inn while one looks into his jug, in Adriaen van Ostade's etching from about 1648.
about: Three peasant men sit around a small table in a dim inn. One wears a tricorn hat and leans in to watch another, who looks down into his jug. A fireplace arch fills the back wall. Adriaen van Ostade etched the scene around 1648. The collector Fritz Rumpf of Potsdam owned this impression until a sale in Leipzig in 1928, when Lessing J. Rosenwald bought it. Rosenwald gave it to the National Gallery of Art in 1943.
dimensions: sheet (trimmed to plate mark): 10.4 × 8.9 cm (4 1/8 × 3 1/2 in.)

meta: A standing woman balances a water jug on her shoulder in Augustin Pajou's drawing after an ancient statue, bought by the National Gallery of Art in 1999.
about: A standing woman in classical drapery balances a large water jug on her shoulder and holds a long staff in her other hand. Augustin Pajou drew her in black chalk with gray wash. He wrote d'après l'antique at lower right, which means after the antique, and Villa Ludov. at lower left, so he copied a statue at the Villa Ludovisi. The Galerie Cailleux in Paris sold the drawing to the National Gallery of Art in 1999.

meta: Rembrandt's Saint Bartholomew, painted in 1661, shows the apostle as a pensive ordinary man holding a knife. It is in the Getty Museum.
about: Saint Bartholomew rests his chin on one hand and looks lost in thought. In his other hand he holds a knife. That is a nod to his martyrdom, since he was skinned alive. The Getty thinks one of Rembrandt's neighbors may have posed for him. Rembrandt painted it only eight years before his own death. By making the apostle a common man, the museum suggests, he gave holiness a human quality that fits the religious mood of mid-1600s Amsterdam.

meta: A priest talks with a young woman at a stone doorway in Théophile Alexandre Steinlen's 1899 drawing Penitence, made for a text by Georges Courteline.
about: A clergyman in a black cassock and wide hat speaks with a young woman at a stone doorway. She wears a patterned shawl, a blue skirt and a white headscarf. Houses of a village show at the right edge. Steinlen made the drawing with brush and ink and colored crayon in 1899. In blue at the lower right he wrote Penitence par Georges Courteline, so it belongs to a piece by that writer.

meta: Guillaume Courtois's red chalk Adoration of the Magi, about 1665, was a finished study for an engraving in a Roman missal.
about: The three Magi bring gifts to the baby Jesus while excited onlookers crowd around. The Virgin sits on a fluted column and a Doric column stands behind the stable, which the Getty reads as a sign of Courtois's classical leanings. Courtois made this highly finished study for an engraving in a book printed in Rome in 1662. That missal carried engravings after drawings by leading painters working in Italy. Most showed Gospel scenes.

meta: Lucas Cranach the Elder's Christ washing the feet of the apostles, 1537, from a Passion cycle for the Hohenzollern court church in Cölln.
about: Christ kneels on a tiled floor to wash the foot of a seated apostle while the other disciples gather round. This is one panel of a large Passion cycle with 14 main panels. Cranach the Elder designed it and signed it with his snake, but his son and the workshop carried it out. Elector Joachim II of Brandenburg wanted it for the church of the dissolved Dominican monastery in Cölln. It would replace the old altars. The model was the Halle Cathedral set of Passion altars that Cardinal Albrecht ordered from Cranach.
